title: Valve Vegetations Compared: Infective, Libman-Sacks, Marantic, and Carcinoid Heart Disease

steps.tx: Infective endocarditis is characterized by large, bulky, highly friable, irregular **infective endocarditic vegetations** situated along lines of valve closure that frequently spill onto adjacent mural endocardium and chordae tendineae. Microscopically, the vegetation consists of dense layers of fibrin and aggregated platelets teeming with embedded colonies of viable bacteria or fungi, surrounded by an intense infiltrate of viable and degenerate neutrophils. The invasive microbial enzymes and intense suppurative inflammation directly destroy underlying valve architecture, causing leaflet ulceration, cusp perforation, and rupture of chordae tendineae.
steps.say: Infective endocarditis produces bulky, friable, destructive vegetations along the lines of valve closure. Under the microscope, these vegetations are composed of layered platelets and fibrin packed with dense clusters of proliferating bacteria or fungi and necrotic neutrophils. Microbial proteases eat through the leaflet collagen, causing leaflet tears, full-thickness perforations, and ruptured chordae tendineae that lead to acute, severe valvular regurgitation.

left.title: Infective Endocarditis Vegetations
points: Bulky, irregular, highly friable masses (up to 2 cm)
Teeming with proliferating bacterial or fungal colonies
Causes destructive leaflet perforation and chordal rupture
High risk of septic emboli producing metastatic abscesses

right.title: Non-Bacterial Vegetations (NBTE)
points: Small (1 to 5 mm), smooth, bland, sterile nodules
Composed purely of platelets and fibrin without organisms
Underlying valve leaflet tissue remains completely undamaged
High risk of sterile bland ischemic emboli to brain/viscera

steps.tx: Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis, historically termed **marantic endocarditis**, is characterized by the deposition of small, bland, sterile thrombi on cardiac valve leaflets. Vegetations measure one to five millimeters in diameter, appearing as smooth, glistening, reddish-brown nodules loosely attached along the lines of closure, most frequently on mitral and aortic valves. Histologically, they consist purely of platelets and fibrin meshworks devoid of microorganisms or significant inflammatory infiltrates. NBTE develops in hypercoagulable states, classically associated with advanced mucinous adenocarcinomas (Trousseau syndrome) and severe debilitating chronic sepsis.
steps.say: Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis, or marantic endocarditis, presents with small, bland, sterile clots on heart valves. The vegetations are small, smooth nodules that sit along the lines of valve closure, usually on mitral or aortic valves. Crucially, they contain only platelets and fibrin: there are no bacteria and no inflammatory cells. Marantic endocarditis is driven by systemic hypercoagulability, classically in advanced cancer like pancreatic adenocarcinoma, known as Trousseau syndrome.

rows: Severe destruction: ulceration, perforation, chordal rupture
Pure platelets and fibrin; sterile, no inflammation
Zero destruction; underlying valve completely intact
Valvulitis with mucoid degeneration and fibrosis
Sterile platelet-fibrin verrucae along closure line
Fibrous commissural fusion and chordal shortening

steps.tx: Although vegetations in non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis do not invade or destroy the underlying valve leaflet tissue, they carry a formidable clinical hazard: **systemic arterial embolization**. Because marantic vegetations are attached very loosely to the denuded endothelial surface without eliciting an anchoring inflammatory reaction, they readily detach under arterial hemodynamic shear stress. Fragmented bland emboli travel through systemic circulation to occlude medium and small arteries, causing acute ischemic cerebral infarcts, splenic infarcts, renal cortical infarcts, and acute mesenteric ischemia in cancer patients.
steps.say: Even though marantic vegetations do not destroy the heart valve itself, they are dangerous because they are very loosely attached to the leaflet surface. Because there is no inflammatory reaction anchoring them to the valve, the swirling blood easily breaks them off into the arterial stream. These sterile emboli travel to the brain, kidneys, and spleen, causing sudden strokes and wedge-shaped infarcts in patients with advanced cancer.

vis.alt: Gross appearance of non-bacterial thrombotic vegetations loosely attached along the mitral valve closure line
vis.caption: Valve substrate pathology predisposing to vegetation formation and regurgitation.

steps.tx: Libman-Sacks endocarditis, also termed verrucous endocarditis, is a sterile, non-infective valvulitis occurring in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and primary antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. The hallmark lesions are small, one to four millimeter, sterile, wart-like, pink-tan **verrucous Libman-Sacks vegetations**. A pathognomonic diagnostic feature is their atypical anatomical distribution: vegetations develop on both flow and non-flow surfaces of valve leaflets, on the undersurfaces of atrioventricular valves, on chordae tendineae, and on adjacent mural endocardium.
steps.say: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is a sterile, wart-like valvular lesion that develops in systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome. What makes Libman-Sacks unique is its bizarre distribution: while ordinary endocarditis sits along lines of closure, Libman-Sacks vegetations sprout on both the upper and lower surfaces of valve leaflets, on chordae tendineae, and on the ventricular wall. Microscopically, they show fibrinoid necrosis and distinctive hematoxylin bodies.

left.title: Libman-Sacks Distribution
points: Both flow and non-flow surfaces of valve leaflets
Undersurfaces of atrioventricular valve cusps
Chordae tendineae and ventricular mural endocardium
Strongly associated with high-titer antiphospholipid antibodies

right.title: Classic Endocarditis Distribution
points: Confined strictly to lines of valve closure
Atrial surface of atrioventricular valves
Ventricular surface of semilunar aortic/pulmonary valves
Dictated by downstream low-pressure vortex flow

steps.tx: Carcinoid heart disease is a unique cardiac manifestation occurring in over fifty percent of patients with metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoid tumours of the gastrointestinal tract that have metastasized to the liver. Neoplastic enterochromaffin cells hypersecrete bioactive amines, predominantly serotonin, bradykinin, and prostaglandins, directly into hepatic veins. These humoral mediators stimulate valvular subendothelial smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts to synthesize **plaque-like carcinoid fibrous thickening**, composed of smooth muscle cells embedded in abundant glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix, coating the tricuspid and pulmonary valves.
steps.say: Carcinoid heart disease develops when neuroendocrine carcinoid tumors metastasize to the liver, dumping large amounts of serotonin and bradykinin directly into the hepatic veins. These vasoactive mediators bathe the right side of the heart, stimulating fibroblasts to deposit glistening, white fibrous plaques on the tricuspid and pulmonary valves. This causes severe tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis, leading to right-sided heart failure.

vis.alt: Gross specimen showing glistening white fibrous plaques coating the tricuspid valve leaflets in carcinoid heart disease
vis.caption: Valve haemodynamic progression, contrasting left sided rheumatic disease with right sided carcinoid fibrosis.

steps.tx: The striking clinical hallmark of carcinoid heart disease is its strict **right-sided valvular predilection**, producing severe tricuspid valve regurgitation and pulmonary valve stenosis while sparing the left side of the heart. As blood traverses pulmonary capillary beds, pulmonary endothelial monoamine oxidase (MAO) and vascular carboxypeptidases rapidly catabolize serotonin and bradykinin into inactive metabolites (such as 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, 5-HIAA). Consequently, left-sided valves remain entirely normal unless the patient possesses a right-to-left intracardiac shunt (patent foramen ovale) or primary pulmonary carcinoid tumour.
steps.say: Carcinoid heart disease almost exclusively damages the right side of the heart. The explanation is physiological: as blood passes through the lungs, pulmonary endothelial monoamine oxidase metabolizes and inactivates serotonin before it can reach the left heart. Therefore, the mitral and aortic valves are completely spared, unless the patient has a patent foramen ovale allowing serotonin to bypass the pulmonary filter, or has a primary lung carcinoid.

rows: Direct exposure to hepatic venous serotonin
Serotonin converted to inactive 5-HIAA in lungs

steps.tx: Clinical and microbiological confirmation of infective endocarditis utilizes the **modified Duke diagnostic criteria**, integrating clinical, microbiological, and echocardiographic parameters. Definite infective endocarditis requires two major criteria, one major and three minor criteria, or five minor criteria. The major criteria comprise persistently positive blood cultures with typical microorganisms (such as viridans streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus, or Staphylococcus aureus) and echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement (oscillating intracardiac mass/vegetation, myocardial ring abscess, or new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve).
steps.say: We confirm infective endocarditis using the modified Duke criteria. Definite endocarditis requires two major criteria, or one major plus three minor criteria. The two major criteria are persistently positive blood cultures drawn separately with typical organisms like viridans streptococci or Staph aureus, and echocardiographic confirmation of an oscillating vegetation, an annular abscess, or new dehiscence of a prosthetic valve.

steps.tx: Successful eradication of infective endocarditis requires four to six weeks of high-dose, parenteral, **bactericidal antimicrobial regimens**. Because microorganisms reside embedded within dense avascular fibrin-platelet vegetations, host phagocytic neutrophils cannot penetrate the lesion, rendering bacteriostatic antibiotics ineffective. Native valve endocarditis caused by viridans streptococci is treated with intravenous aqueous penicillin G or ceftriaxone, often combined with synergistic gentamicin. Staphylococcus aureus native valve endocarditis requires intravenous flucloxacillin or nafcillin for methicillin-sensitive strains, and intravenous vancomycin or daptomycin for MRSA.
steps.say: Treating infective endocarditis requires prolonged, intravenous bactericidal antibiotic therapy for four to six weeks. Because bacteria are shielded deep within an avascular fortress of fibrin and platelets, host neutrophils cannot reach them, so bacteriostatic agents fail. Native valve viridans streptococci are treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone. Staphylococcus aureus requires flucloxacillin, or vancomycin if methicillin-resistant, monitoring blood cultures daily until clearance is confirmed.

left.title: Medical Antimicrobial Therapy
points: Parenteral bactericidal agents for 4 to 6 weeks
Penicillin G or ceftriaxone for viridans streptococci
Vancomycin or flucloxacillin for staphylococci
Monitors daily blood cultures to confirm clearance

right.title: Indications for Urgent Surgery
points: Acute refractory congestive heart failure
Persistent bacteremia despite 7-10 days of therapy
Fungal endocarditis or multi-drug resistant strains
Annular ring abscess or large mobile vegetation >10 mm

quiz.q: Which anatomical distribution of valvular vegetations is unique to Libman-Sacks endocarditis in systemic lupus erythematosus?
options: Vegetations develop on both flow and non-flow surfaces, chordae tendineae, and mural endocardium
Vegetations are strictly confined to the lines of closure on the atrial surface of the mitral valve
Vegetations develop exclusively on the ventricular surface of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Vegetations are confined strictly to the tricuspid valve leaflets with pulmonary stenosis
quiz.explain: Libman-Sacks vegetations uniquely appear on both upper and lower surfaces of valve leaflets, on chordae tendineae, and on adjacent mural endocardium, unlike other endocarditis forms.

quiz.q: Why is carcinoid heart disease almost exclusively restricted to the right-sided cardiac valves (tricuspid and pulmonary)?
options: Circulating serotonin is catabolized by pulmonary endothelial monoamine oxidase before reaching the left heart
The left ventricle generates high systolic shear forces that wash away serotonin receptor complexes
The pulmonary valve possesses specialized serotonin receptors lacking on the aortic valve
Enterochromaffin tumor cells embolize directly to the right ventricular myocardium alone
quiz.explain: Pulmonary endothelial cells express monoamine oxidase (MAO), which rapidly metabolizes serotonin into inactive 5-HIAA as blood passes through the lungs, sparing the left-sided valves.

quiz.q: What microscopic feature distinguishes non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (marantic endocarditis) from infective endocarditis?
options: Sterile vegetations composed purely of platelets and fibrin without inflammatory cells or microorganisms
Dense colonies of gram-positive cocci embedded in an intense neutrophilic infiltrate
Granulomatous Aschoff bodies with central fibrinoid necrosis and caterpillar cells
Large myxomatous collections of basophilic glycosaminoglycans expanding the spongiosa
quiz.explain: Marantic endocarditis vegetations are sterile, bland thrombi made purely of platelets and fibrin, completely lacking microorganisms or underlying destructive valve inflammation.
